How to reason about Beacon Lattice placements

Use piece shapes, rotations, corners, and leftover regions to reason about Beacon Lattice’s exact-cover puzzle without assuming a hint system.

By NoCharge·Reviewed by NoCharge·Published August 19, 2026·Updated November 24, 2026·2 min read
Try the detail in a live board.

Cover every cell. Overlap nothing.

Play Beacon LatticeBrowse all Articles

Bottom line: Beacon Lattice is a five-piece tiling puzzle. Reason about which remaining pentominoes can cover each open region; the game does not provide old-style coverage counters, restricted slots, or a forced-move hint.

The five-by-five board begins empty. Your inventory contains F, V, I, U, and L pieces, each made of five connected squares. Every piece must be placed once, and every board square must be covered exactly once.

Start with constrained squares

A corner or a narrow edge can be more informative than the open center because fewer piece orientations can reach it. For each remaining shape, consider its allowed quarter-turns and anchors. If only one legal shape-and-anchor combination can cover a particular open square, that placement is forced by the puzzle’s constraints—not by a built-in clue.

Check the space left behind

After a placement, look at the shape of the remaining open area. A disconnected region smaller than five squares cannot be filled by a five-cell piece. A one-cell gap or a narrow notch may also make the remaining inventory impossible to fit. This is a reason to undo and reconsider an earlier placement, not a reason to overlap another piece.

Track the inventory and orientation

Each piece is distinct and can rotate in quarter turns; the current game does not offer a reflection control. Keep track of which piece has been used and which orientations still fit. The row and column selectors make an anchor explicit, while the board rejects overlaps and placements that extend beyond an edge.

Use the controls that exist

Undo placement removes the most recent accepted piece and restores it to the inventory. Reset to seeded start restores the empty lattice and all five pieces. There are no locked starting pieces, restricted-slot rules, stored bests, or automatic forced-placement detector in the current game.

See the exact-cover explanation for the win condition, or open the current Beacon Lattice page to play.
